blocks.x: Digital twin of the melt shop, energy per ton down 8.5% and ladle-return temperature variance cut by a third

A steel producer: Plants feel data gaps in scrap rates and unplanned downtime, both traceable to decisions made hours earlier. The Achala program started at the line —. The baseline signed in week two made the cost visible in units the finance team already owns, and the engagement ran under the standard Achala charter — a named metric, a named control owner and gates that evidence every move.

The baseline quarter measured the folklore: energy per ton varied 14% between shifts running the same grades, and no one could say which practice was actually cheaper because the data arrived per-shift in formats no system joined.
Setpoint changes were reasoned from experience and logged nowhere. The energy team's improvement cases died for lack of a baseline anyone trusted.

We built the melt-shop twin: sensor streams from furnace, ladle and casting normalized into one process model, shift practices quantified against energy per ton with the foremen's knowledge encoded as comparables rather than replaced, and recommendation gates putting every setpoint suggestion in an operator-approved loop. The improvement backlog now ranks itself by measured delta.
